title: Behavioral contract and lossy compatibility gateway for OpenAI Responses mapping
creator: Avery Chen
description:
Summary: Design a runtime translation layer (compatibility gateway) that maps Redwood's Responses surface to OpenAI Responses semantics while exposing a configurable 'behavioral contract' allowing teams to choose fidelity levels (strict, permissive, lossy). This ticket covers the API-level mapping decisions, event translation rules for streaming/tool-calling/structured-output, failure and fallback policies, and the rollout/canary plan.

Problem statement: Customers using the OpenAI Responses contract expect certain streaming event shapes, function/tool invocation handshakes, and JSON-structured outputs that differ subtly from our native runtime events. Edge cases cause behavior deltas: ordering of tool-invocation vs. partial tokens, presence/absence of role fields in deltas, differing finish_reason semantics, and mismatches for structured output validation failures. These deltas break integrations and generated-sample tests for some customers.

Goals:
- Define a precise mapping matrix for streaming event types (delta tokens, tool_call start/complete, metadata events) and structured output translations.
- Implement a pluggable gateway with three fidelity modes: 
  1) strict — emulate OpenAI Responses exactly where possible (add synthetic events where needed),
  2) permissive — best-effort mapping while keeping native runtime efficiency,
  3) lossy — lowest-overhead mapping that may elide non-essential events for latency/cost.
- Provide runtime flags, observability (per-request mapping trace), and regression tests (prompt-driven suites) to detect behavior drift.

Design notes / mapping highlights:
- Streaming deltas: Our runtime emits token deltas and structured patches. For strict mode, gateway must coalesce deltas into OpenAI-compatible 'delta' objects and insert role/content keys even for token fragments. For permissive mode, emit our native stream and add a compatibility wrapper only at EOF. Lossy mode omits wrapper overhead to minimize tail latency.
- Tool/function calling: OpenAI's model->tool handshake expects an event sequence "tool_call.start" -> tool execution -> "tool_call.exec" with embedded args. Our runtime currently emits a single "invoke_tool" event. Gateway will synthesize start/exec pairs for strict mode and attach deterministic IDs. We must preserve deterministic replayability (important for deduping and cache keys).
- Structured outputs: OpenAI uses function outputs (name + arguments JSON). When we detect schema mismatches we can either 1) emit a structured error event with "finish_reason"="function_error" (strict), 2) return best-effort parsed JSON with annotations (permissive), or 3) return raw string and log a schema-violation metric (lossy).
- Finish reasons and stop tokens: Map our internal stop semantics to OpenAI finish_reason values. When ambiguous, strict mode should insert an explicit "stop" event with the nearest token index.

Trade-offs:
- Latency: Strict mode increases per-request CPU and increases serialization overhead (approx +3–12ms median on microbenchmarks).
- Complexity: Synthetic events add code paths and invariants to maintain; risk of subtle ordering bugs in streaming.
- Observability vs. privacy: Detailed mapping traces aid debugging but surface internal metadata; tracing must be opt-in or redacted for private deployments.

Implementation plan:
1) Spec: produce the mapping matrix and event transformation rules (this ticket). Link to spec: https://redwood.atlassian.com/confluence/display/API/OpenAI+Responses+Mapping+Matrix (draft).
2) Prototype: add a translation library in runtime/compat with strict/permissive/lossy modes. Add unit tests that run prompt suites and compare against OpenAI golden traces.
3) Load test: run streaming load with strict mode at 50% traffic in a canary pool to measure tail latency and error rates.
4) Rollout: phased canary -> customer opt-in -> default to permissive -> opt-out for private customers.

Acceptance criteria:
- Mapping matrix accepted by PM and DX.
- E2E regression suite (100+ prompts) passes with strict mode for 95% of golden traces.
- Observability surfaces per-request mapping decisions and counts of lossy degradations.
- Canary running at 5% traffic for 2 weeks without customer-facing regressions.

comments: 2026-02-12 - Avery Chen: Created ticket after customer incident where function-calling handshake differed and caused SDK retry loops. Draft spec attached to description.

2026-02-16 - Diego Martins: Initial spike completed. Prototype can synthesize start/exec events but increases median latency by ~4ms in strict mode. Uploaded microbenchmark results to the eval dashboard.
2026-02-20 - PM feedback (Leah O'Neill): Request to add an explicit 'fidelity' parameter to the public API and to include migration guidance for customers relying on event ordering. Added to spec.
2026-02-25 - Design feedback (Ravi Patel): UX for console should show per-request mapping annotations and allow toggling fidelity for saved routes. Filed design ticket DES-412 for console controls.

2026-03-03 - Engineering note (Diego Martins): Found an ordering race when streaming tool output and token deltas concurrently; mitigated by sequencing layer that tags events with monotonic sequence IDs. Added tests in runtime/compat/tests.
2026-03-08 - Security (Maya Singh): Raised concerns about exposing internal model IDs in mapping traces. Decided to redact ids for Private deployments; added config flag 'compat.redact_internal_ids'.
2026-03-10 - QA (Nina Alvarez): Regression suite results: strict mode matched 93/100 golden traces. Investigating 7 failures (mostly structured-output edge cases due to nested arrays).
2026-03-12 - Diego Martins: Implemented permissive & lossy flags, added metrics (compat.lossy_count, compat.strict_mismatch). Preparing canary config for runtime-1.22.
2026-03-12 - Next steps: Schedule canary (5%) for 2026-03-20, complete remaining structured-output fixes, and publish migration guide.
